title: Puppy Barking: Why It Happens and What to Do
description: Why puppies bark, how to work out the reason, and calm ways to reduce it without scolding. Practical steps for new owners.

quick: Barking is normal communication, and puppies bark for many reasons: play, alerting, fear, boredom, attention or being alone. Work out why your puppy is barking, meet the need, and reward quiet. ASPCA warns that a puppy who is rewarded for barking learns to bark more, and there is no quick fix, so be consistent.

faq.q: Why does my puppy bark so much?
faq.a: Common reasons are excitement or play, alerting to sounds, fear of new things, boredom, wanting attention, or distress when alone. Pain or illness can also be a cause, so see your vet if the barking is new or unusual.

faq.q: Should I ignore a barking puppy?
faq.a: It depends on the reason. ASPCA says that if a dog gets what he wants by barking, he learns to bark for it, so do not hand over attention at the moment of barking. But never ignore a puppy who needs the toilet, is scared, or is in distress.

faq.q: Will shouting stop my puppy barking?
faq.a: Usually not. PDSA advises not getting angry at a dog that barks, because it can upset them more. Work on the cause and reward calm behaviour.

faq.q: Will my puppy grow out of barking?
faq.a: Barking is a normal dog behaviour, so it will not go away completely. ASPCA says that it takes time to teach a dog to bark less, and that expecting a quick fix or total silence is unrealistic.

faq.q: What is alarm barking in puppies?
faq.a: ASPCA describes alarm barking as barking at any and every noise or sight regardless of context, usually with stiffer body language than a greeting bark. Reward calm behaviour and avoid scolding.

faq.q: Is it normal for puppies to bark when they greet people?
faq.a: Yes. ASPCA says a dog that barks at people or dogs with a relaxed body, excitement and a wagging tail may be greeting. Teach an alternative such as sitting before the greeting.

html:
The doorbell rings and your puppy launches into a squeaky, wobbly, very determined bark. It is cute for a day, then you start to worry about the neighbours. The good news is that barking is normal, and you can shape it with a few consistent habits.

Why puppies bark

ASPCA explains that barking is a natural part of how dogs communicate, and many owners can tell the reason from the sound. A bark that means "play with me" sounds different from one that means "let me in". Common causes in puppies are:

  • Excitement and play, especially in the evening when puppies get the zoomies. See puppy zoomies.
  • Alerting, to the doorbell, footsteps or noises outside.
  • Fear or uncertainty, about new people, objects or sounds. PDSA says that a well-socialised puppy is less likely to be afraid or unsure of everything when older.
  • Wanting attention, food or a walk.
  • Boredom or too little exercise.
  • Being alone, which can come with whining and pacing. Read our guide to puppy separation anxiety.
  • Pain or illness, which is why sudden barking is worth a vet check.

The main types of barking

ASPCA describes several patterns, and knowing which one you have makes the fix much easier.

TypeWhat it looks like
TerritorialBarking at people, dogs or animals within or approaching the dog's territory
AlarmBarking at any noise or sight, with stiffer body language, often moving forward an inch or two with each bark
Attention-seekingBarking at people or animals to get attention, food, toys or play
GreetingBarking at people or dogs with a relaxed body, excitement and a wagging tail, sometimes with whining
CompulsiveRepetitive, like a broken record, often with repetitive movement such as pacing

PDSA's vets add that barking is a normal behaviour used for greeting, as part of play, as a warning and for many other reasons. It becomes a problem when owners feel the dog is barking too much, or when the dog is becoming distressed while barking. That second case is a reason to look at fear, loneliness or health, not just volume.

Barking and socialisation

PDSA says that a dog that has been well socialised as a puppy, with a range of new things experienced positively, is less likely to be afraid or unsure of everything when older. So gentle, early exposure to sights, sounds and smells is one of the best long-term ways to cut fear barking. Use the socialization checklist and see where your puppy is in our development stages guide.

A simple daily plan to reduce barking

  1. Morning: a walk or play session suited to your puppy's age, then a chew or food toy.
  2. Peak barking times: block the view, give a task, and reward a quiet moment right away.
  3. Visitors: reward your puppy for sitting or staying calm before you open the door.
  4. Evening: a calm routine, a toilet break, and a quiet place to sleep, as in our guide to puppy crying at night.

Keep notes on how often barking happens each day. Progress is slow, and a log shows it. ASPCA is clear that it takes time to teach a dog to bark less, so aim for steady improvement.

Step 1: Work out why

ASPCA says that to reduce barking it is crucial to determine why the dog is barking. Keep a note for three days: when it happens, what came just before, and what your puppy got afterwards. You will often see a pattern, such as barking when you are on a call, or when your puppy has been in the crate too long.

Step 2: Meet the need

ReasonWhat helps
Needs the toiletTake your puppy out. See our potty schedule
Bored or full of energyAge-appropriate play, a chew or food toy, short training games
Fear of new soundsGentle, positive exposure at a distance your puppy can handle
Barking at nightCheck the basics in puppy crying at night
Tired and overstimulatedA calm break and a nap in a quiet place

Step 3: Do not reward the barking

ASPCA says that barking is rewarded when it gets the dog what it wants, and dogs who successfully bark for attention often go on to bark for food, play and walks. So wait for a pause in the barking, then give attention, a treat or the door opening. If your puppy learns that quiet gets things, quiet becomes the better option.

The ASPCA also recommends teaching a quiet cue, so you can ask for another behaviour such as sit instead. Start with an easy moment, say "quiet" when the puppy pauses for a second, and reward straight away. Make it longer as your puppy gets the idea.

Step 4: Prevent practice

Every time a puppy barks and gets a result, the habit gets stronger. Block the view of the street with a gate or curtains, keep the puppy away from the window during peak times, and offer a chew or food toy in busy moments. Use a calm crate or pen routine for rest.

What not to do

  • Do not shout. PDSA says that getting angry at a dog that barks will upset them even more.
  • Do not scold a fearful puppy. Fear needs distance and gentle exposure, not a telling off.
  • Do not expect silence. ASPCA says the aim is less barking, not none.

When to ask for help

If barking comes with signs of panic, destruction, or hurting themselves, or if it starts suddenly, talk to your vet or an accredited behaviourist. The cause may be medical or a bigger anxiety issue. Otherwise, with patience, most puppies learn that quiet works.

Teach quiet: step by step

  1. Pick a calm moment with few distractions and a handful of small treats.
  2. Wait for a pause in the barking, even one second.
  3. Say your quiet cue and reward immediately, while the puppy is still quiet.
  4. Add time slowly. Reward after two seconds, then five, then longer.
  5. Ask for another behaviour, such as sit, as ASPCA suggests, so your puppy has something to do instead of barking.
  6. Practice in real life, at the door, at the window or when you get ready for a walk.

When barking points to something else

PDSA says the real issue is often not the sound itself, but whether the dog is distressed. If your puppy barks with panic, pacing or destruction while alone, read about separation anxiety. If barking starts suddenly, is very different from normal, or comes with other changes in behaviour, mention it to your vet, since pain or illness can change how a dog acts.
